content:
President Donald Trump on Sunday harshly criticised the "mess" White House he inherited when he returned to the White House, using a word he had publicly denied using to describe the building in 2017.

Trump posted on his "Truth Social" platform to defend his White House renovation plans, claiming that before he returned to the executive residence, the White House was in "terrible condition both inside and out".

"To be honest, it really was a 'mess'! No president has properly taken care of it," he wrote.

"I enjoy renovating this place during my spare time, though I don't really have much spare time," the president continued. According to didtrumpgolftoday.com statistics, out of the 603 days of his second term, he has played golf on 136 days, with estimated taxpayer-funded costs reaching US$190 million.

Trump posted at a time when his "beautification" projects in Washington, D.C. have faced continuous criticism from local residents. The post comes nine years after he slammed "fake news" over a report nine years ago — a report that claimed he had told members of his frequently-visited golf club in Bedminster, New Jersey, that the reason he frequented the golf course was because the White House "really is a mess".

"I love the White House, it is one of the most beautiful buildings (residences) I have ever seen. But the fake news saying I described it as a mess — that is completely wrong," he wrote on X (formerly Twitter) in 2017.

Alan Shipnuck, the author of that over-7,000-word report for Sports Illustrated, insisted his reporting was accurate after then-White House Director of Strategic Communications Hope Hicks asked him to retract the story.

Shipnuck said at the time on a Golf.com podcast: "I explained to her that this was not a lie. The president said it in front of eight or nine members and staff at the Bedminster club."

"It was his first time back at the club after moving into the White House, and it was a candid moment. One of the people there relayed this to me. I found this person to be a very credible source on many topics."

He described the "mess" comment as having become "a legendary moment" at that golf course.

"This comment may have inconvenienced his boss, and he might wish his boss had never said it, but it is not a lie," he said.
